title: Grid Minimum Path Sum With Doubling Rule

reported.text: Grid minimum path sum (right/down moves only) with an extra doubling rule that depends on parity.

sources.passage:
Infosys DSE/SP OA 2026 (Aug 06, Slot 1) — Reconstructed Problems and Discussion
I appeared for the Infosys DSE/SP programming assessment today and am sharing the problems I remember for learning and discussion. The statements are reconstructed from memory, so some details may be incomplete.

1. Clipping Points in an Array
   An internal element is a clipping point if it is either greater than both neighbours or smaller than both neighbours. Remove one element so that the number of remaining clipping points is minimum.

Example:
[1, 5, 2, 4, 3]

The clipping points are 5, 2 and 4. Removing 2 gives [1, 5, 4, 3], which has only one clipping point.


2. Stock Buy and Sell with Variable Cooldown
   After buying on day b and selling on day s, the cooldown period was based on the holding duration:

s - b + 1

The objective was to maximize total profit.

3. Grid Minimum Path Sum with Parity Rule
   Move only right or down from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. Maintain a running sum, and apply an additional doubling rule when the relevant values have the same parity.

This likely requires grid DP with parity as an additional state.

4. Music Playlist DP
   The problem involved creating a playlist of a given goal length with n songs and a value k controlling when a song could be repeated. This seemed similar to LeetCode 920, Number of Music Playlists.

reported.text: A playlist-counting DP similar to LeetCode 920, Number of Music Playlists.

title: Largest Value on Both Sides of a Peak

reported.text: An array has a peak; find the largest value that appears on both sides of it.

sources.passage:
Infosys OA Off-Campus || 1st August
It consisted of 3 problems: `Easy`, `Easy`, `Medium`.

For the role of Specialist Programmer (Trainee) and Digital Specialist Engineer (Trainee).

## First Problem:

Given an array with a peak (it always exists). Now you have to find the maximum element that exists on both the left and right of the peak.

`N <= 1e5`
`a[i] <= 1e9`

### Solution:

Find the maximum element index. Now use a `set` to store the elements from the left side `[0, maximumElementIndex)`, and then check which element exists in the right range and take the maximum `(maximumElementIndex, n - 1]`.

## Second Problem:

Given an array consisting of positive, negative, and zero values, you can change the sign of at most one element. Find the maximum sum subarray.

`N <= 1e5`
`abs(a[i]) <= 1e9`

### Solution:

Since this is a maximum sum subarray problem, think about `Kadane's` algorithm. But the normal version will not work.

If I am at the current element, then I would change the negative one. Now I want the maximum sum subarray that we can get from the left and the right.

Use prefix/suffix arrays to find the maximum subarray ending at index `i` from the forward and backward directions.

Now, for each index, do `Left[i - 1] + Right[i + 1] + abs(current)`.

## Third Problem:

Given an array and `K`, divide the array into `K` contiguous subarrays. The cost of a subarray is `maximum - minimum of subarray` + `abs(left end - right end)`. Find the minimum cost among all partitions.

`N <= 500`
`K <= N`

### Solution:

For the recursive approach, we need 3 parameters: `fun(index, Segments, prevIndex)`.

We can further reduce this by defining the state:

Let `dp[i][k]` return the minimum cost sum for the first `i` elements with exactly `k` segments.

Now, assume the last subarray starts at index `j`.

We would have the transition as: `dp[i][k] = dp[j - 1][k - 1] + cost(i, j)`.

This can be done in `O(N^3 log N)` or `O(N^3)` time complexity.

title: Split Array Into K Parts at Minimum Cost

reported.text: Split an array (N <= 500) into K contiguous parts; each part costs (max - min) + |left end - right end|. Minimise the total cost.
